unit-4.grownUpGuide.sections.0.body:
Hello, and welcome to Global Perspectives at Ehel Academy. This guide is written for you, the grown-up, whether you are a teacher in a class or a parent at home. You will lead these lessons together with your child, side by side.

Global Perspectives is a little different from other subjects. It is not about learning long lists of facts. It is about growing thinking skills that a child will use for the whole of their life. In this unit, the topic is fairness, but the real gift is helping your child learn to think, to compare, and to give reasons.

The big question of this unit is simple but powerful: what does it mean to be fair? Along the way your child will explore needs and wants, and a kind idea called fair trade — the idea that the farmers who grow our food should get a fair price for their hard work.
grownUpGuide.sections.1.items: Comparing — noticing what is the same and what is different, such as a need compared with a want, or something fair compared with something not fair.
Judging what is fair — looking at a real situation and deciding if it is fair, and beginning to say why.
Giving reasons — using the words 'I think ... because ...' to explain an opinion out loud.
unit-4.grownUpGuide.sections.8.body:
Aim: to help your child feel what the word 'fair' means.

Talk about: Take a snack you can share, such as a mango or some bread. Share it two ways: first give one person a big piece and the other a tiny piece, then share it evenly. Ask: which way felt fair? Why? Talk about times at home or school that felt fair or not fair.

Do: Together, do the 'Is it fair?' activity in the Activity Sheet. Then meet the word charity — giving money, things or time to people who need it. Many families, whether they go to the mosque or the church, teach that sharing and being fair to others is important. Share two friendly views: Amal thinks charity is the very best way to help people in need, because they get what they need quickly. Sami thinks it is even better to help people earn their own money, so they can always buy what they need. Ask your child who they agree with. There is no wrong answer here.
unit-4.grownUpGuide.sections.10.body:
Aim: to learn what fair trade means.

Talk about: First, the word trade — it just means buying and selling things. When Idris buys a banana, that is trade. Now ask: is the farmer who grew the banana being treated fairly? Do they get enough money for all their hard work?

Do: Start a simple KWL chart together on a sheet of paper. Make three columns: K for what we Know, W for what we Want to know, and L for what we have Learned. Write one thing in each. Then teach the key idea below. Fair-trade foods your child may know include bananas, coffee, honey, sesame, mangoes and dates — many grown by farmers in East Africa and other warm places. Keep this chart on the wall or in a folder, and add to the 'Learned' column all through the unit. It is lovely to watch it fill up.
unit-4.grownUpGuide.sections.11.body:
Aim: to find out which foods can be fair trade.

Talk about: Which foods might travel a long way from a farm to reach us? Bananas, coffee, honey, sesame, mangoes, dates, and chocolate are all foods that can be fair trade. Look at any packets you have at home for a fair-trade mark.

Do: Play a quick game of 'Draw it!' — one person draws a fair-trade food and the other guesses it. Then, if you like, make a simple home-made board game together: draw a winding path of squares on a big sheet, write a happy fair-trade step on some squares (such as 'you sell your bananas for a fair price, move on 2') and a setback on others (such as 'a storm hurts your crop, wait a turn'), and use a coin or a stone as a counter. Add any new words to your KWL chart. Introduce the word expert — your child is becoming a real fair-trade expert!
unit-4.grownUpGuide.sections.16.body:
Some children may notice that some families have more than others. Keep the tone warm and hopeful. Focus on what we can do — share, be kind, be fair, and choose fair-trade food when we can — rather than on what anyone lacks. Take care never to make a child feel bad about what their own family has or does not have. If a child shares something personal, simply listen kindly. Being fair starts with being gentle with each other, right here in the room.

Thank you for giving your child this time. The habits they build here — looking closely, comparing fairly, and saying 'I think, because' — will help them for many years, in every subject and far beyond school. Enjoy the unit together.
unit-4.grownUpGuide.sections.9.body:
Aim: to tell the difference between needs and wants.

Talk about: What must we have to stay alive and well? These are needs: food, clean water, a home, clothes, and people who love us. What is only nice to have? These are wants: toys, sweets, games. Wants are lovely, but we can live without them.

Do: Do the 'Needs and wants' sort in the Activity Sheet together. Then tell your child about Amara's family, slowly and with feeling. Talk about how the charity's food helped Amara's family for a short time, but the banana plants and the cooperative helped them for a long time.

unit-5.explainers.0.body:
Amara goes to Ehel Academy in Hargeisa. This year a new girl called Imani joined her class. Imani had just moved from far away, so everything felt new and a little bit scary. On the first morning, Amara walked over and said hello. She learned to say Imani's name, and asked her to sit together. At playtime, she asked Imani to join the game. Soon Imani was smiling. One kind hello made all the difference! In these activities, you will get ready to welcome a new friend, just like Amara did.

After a few days, Imani felt brave enough to share something from home. She taught the class a song her family loved. Everyone joined in, even though the words were new. When we welcome someone, we get a lovely gift back too — we learn about their world.

unit-5.grownUpGuide.sections.0.body:
Welcome to the last unit of Year 3 Global Perspectives at Ehel Academy. This unit is called You are welcome! It is a warm, gentle unit about where our families come from, the special things families pass on, and how we can make a new person feel happy and safe when they join us.

Global Perspectives is a little different from other subjects. It is not about learning lots of facts by heart. It is about growing helpful thinking and caring skills through a real topic. In this unit the topic is family, heritage and welcoming newcomers, and the skills are all about understanding our own story, listening to other people, and being kind.

This is a lovely topic for children in the Horn of Africa. Many of our families have wonderful stories of movement and heritage. Grandparents may have grown up by the sea in Berbera, in a busy city like Mogadishu, or in a small village far from town. Some children have family who came from another country. Every one of these stories is interesting and worth being proud of.

This guide is written for you, the grown-up — the teacher or the parent leading the way. The children are only seven or eight, so you will read, talk and do the activities together. Everything is kept short, simple and picture-led.

The unit builds slowly towards one happy project. After six little lessons, the children make a real welcome for a child who is new to their class — a friendly video, or a bright poster or booklet. So as you go, you are always heading somewhere kind: every lesson adds one more idea about how to make a newcomer feel they belong.
unit-5.grownUpGuide.sections.1.body:
Three big Global Perspectives skills grow in this unit. You do not need to name them for the children — just help them practise:

Along the way children also do a little gentle research (asking family, looking at pictures) and a little working together (making something as a team). But the heart of the unit is kindness and understanding.

Welcoming is a real skill, and it is one of the kindest a child can learn. A newcomer who is met with a warm hello, a learned name and an invitation to play will remember it for years. When children practise this now, they are learning to notice how another person feels and to do something kind about it. That gift stays with them well beyond this unit.

At Ehel Academy, young learners are led by a grown-up. Three kinds of help work together in this unit:

You will also see Ask Your Family boxes. These invite the child to talk to someone at home about the family's story. This is one of the warmest parts of the unit, so give it time and treat every answer as a treasure.

Keep every sitting playful. Chat more than you write, use lots of pictures, and let the child use their home language whenever it helps. If a child wants to teach you a word from home, that is a wonderful moment — celebrate it. The mood you are aiming for is warm, curious and gentle, never a test.

grownUpGuide.sections.5.items: Keep it positive and never political. When we talk about people moving, keep the reasons simple and kind — to be near family, for a new job, to go to school, or to find a happy, safe home.
Let children share only what they want to. Never press a child to talk about their family. A drawing, a single word, or nothing at all is completely fine.
Celebrate every family. A family that has always lived in one town has a story just as special as a family that has travelled far. No story is better than another.
Be even-handed and fair. Children come from different backgrounds and celebrate different special days. Welcome all of them equally and kindly.
Watch for tender moments. If a story brings up a big feeling, pause, be gentle, and move on to something warm. It is always fine to say that some things are private.
unit-5.grownUpGuide.sections.6.body:
To make the unit friendly, we follow one Year 3 child all the way through. Her name is Amara, and she is a learner at Ehel Academy in Hargeisa. Amara loves stories, especially the ones her grandmother tells about growing up near the sea.

This year a new girl has joined Amara's class. Her name is Imani. Amara remembers her own first day and decides she will help Imani feel welcome. As you go through the unit, you will see little moments from Amara and Imani's story.

unit-5.grownUpGuide.sections.13.body: Do. Meet three friends who live in different places. Leila lives in a busy city with tall buildings and markets that seem never to sleep. unit-5.grownUpGuide.sections.20.body:
The unit finishes with a kind, joyful project. In a small team, the children make a welcome for a child who is new to their class — just like Amara welcoming Imani. There are two ways to do it, so pick whichever suits your group:

The full child-friendly, step-by-step plan is in File 3, the Mini-Project and Reflection sheet. Children do it with a grown-up close by. The aim is simple: to make a real newcomer feel happy, safe and glad to be here.

Everything from the earlier lessons feeds in here. The children already know how a newcomer might feel, they have practised kind hellos, and they have thought about what is great about their home. Now they simply put it together into one warm welcome. Encourage them to use their own words, and remind them that a short, honest, kind message is far better than a long or fancy one.

unit-4.explainers.0.body:
Hello, and welcome back to Global Perspectives at Ehel Academy. You have already grown three thinking skills this year. In Research you learned to find things out in a careful way. In Analysis you learned to look closely at a topic and ask why things happen. In Evaluation you learned to weigh a source and decide how far to trust it. Now you reach a skill that is a little different, because it is all about you. It is called Reflection.

Here are all six thinking skills again, so you can see where this unit fits:

The first three skills look outwards, at the world. Reflection is different. It looks inwards, at yourself and at your team. Reflection means stopping after you have done something, looking back honestly, and asking: how well did my team work together, and what did I learn?

So Reflection has two parts. One part is thinking about teamwork — what you did to help your team, the good parts and the hard parts of working together, and how to do better next time. The other part is thinking about your learning — what you found out, how an activity helped you, and how your ideas have changed. This unit grows both.

People reflect all the time, not only in school. A footballer watches the last match to see what to fix. A cook tastes the soup and adds a little more salt next time. A big sister works out how to help her shy little brother feel happy at a party. All of them are looking back and learning. People who do this get better, faster, at almost everything. That is the skill you will start to build here.

Everyone wants to belong. A new pupil on their first day, a visitor from far away, a grandmother at a busy party, a child who speaks a different language — all of them feel happy when someone helps them belong. Your Challenge is to think about the different groups people belong to, and to find warm ways to make others feel welcome. unit-2.explainers.0.body:
Hello, and welcome back to Global Perspectives at Ehel Academy. In Unit 1 you learned your first thinking skill, Research — finding out about the world in a careful, tidy way. Well done for finishing it. Now you are ready for the second skill: Analysis.

Remember, Global Perspectives has six thinking skills. You grow them, little by little, over your years here. This unit is all about the second one:

So what is analysis? Analysis means looking closely at a topic and thinking hard about it. In research, you find things out. In analysis, you look at what you found and ask good questions about it. What do different people think? What is a fact, and what is just an opinion? Why is this happening? What pattern can I see? What would be a fair thing to do?

Why does this matter outside school? Grown-ups analyse every day. A nurse looks at what is making people ill and works out why. A shopkeeper looks at what sells and works out a pattern. A community listens to everyone before it changes a busy road. When you practise analysis now, you are learning to think clearly and be fair for the rest of your life.

unit-5.explainers.0.body:
Welcome to Unit 5 of Global Perspectives at Ehel Academy. By now you know that this subject is not about memorising facts. It teaches you a set of thinking and working skills that you can use for the rest of your life, in any subject and in the real world around you.

There are six skills in Global Perspectives, and you grow all of them over your years here:

This unit is all about the fifth skill: Collaboration. So far, most of your Global Perspectives work has been something you could do largely on your own: researching, analysing, evaluating and reflecting. Collaboration is different. You cannot collaborate by yourself. It is the skill of getting good things done with other people — agreeing a shared goal, sharing the work fairly, listening to each other, handling disagreements kindly, and finishing something together that no single person could have made alone.

You may wonder why this matters beyond school. Almost everything important in the adult world is built by teams. A new clinic is designed by doctors, builders and planners working together. A family wedding in Hargeisa is organised by many relatives sharing tasks. A small shop runs because the owner, the supplier and the staff cooperate. A borehole gets dug because a community agrees on it, funds it and works on it together. People who can collaborate well get chosen for the best work, and they get more done. That is why we practise it on purpose here.

unit-5.explainers.2.body:
In the last unit you followed one learner. Because this unit is about teamwork, we will follow a whole group of Year 7 learners at Ehel Academy in Hargeisa. They are an ordinary team, with ordinary strengths and ordinary disagreements, and you will see exactly how they work through each collaboration skill.

Notice that no one in this group is good at everything, and that is completely normal. A strong team is not made of five people who are all the same. It is made of different people whose strengths fit together, so that the team as a whole can do what no single member could. As you meet each skill, watch how this group uses each person's strength — and how they help Idris, their quietest member, to take part.

You will also watch them disagree, get stuck, and get a few things wrong along the way, because that is what real teams do. What makes them a good team is not that they never struggle. It is that they keep working together kindly, and honestly, until they get there. Your own team will be exactly the same, and that is nothing to worry about.

Not all communication is spoken. Often a visual — a poster, a chart, a diagram or a slogan — carries your message faster than words alone. A good visual is not decoration; it helps the audience understand something more quickly.

Two visual tools are especially useful in Global Perspectives:
explainers.11.bullets: Simple charts — a bar chart or table can show a number pattern in a second, far faster than a sentence. If your evidence is numbers, a chart is often the clearest choice.
Slogans — a short, memorable phrase that raises awareness of an issue. Slogans work because they are short, so people remember them.

Friendly register — warm and simple, still respectful. Suits younger audiences, family, or awareness posters.

Verbal feedback — short spoken signals such as 'I see', 'I understand' and 'that makes sense'.

Research is finding out about something in a careful, organised way, from several sources, so that you can trust what you learn, weigh different perspectives, and explain it to someone else. It is not just typing a question into a search engine. Real research means asking a focused question that can be debated, gathering information from a range of sources, judging and cross-checking them, recording the important parts in your own words, synthesising them into your own findings, and saying where everything came from.

Three habits sit at its heart. Always use more than one source, because one source can be wrong or one-sided. unit-5.explainers.0.body:
Hello, and welcome to Unit 5 of Global Perspectives at Ehel Academy. By now you know this subject is not about memorising facts. It teaches you a set of thinking and working skills that you can carry into any subject, any job, and any part of your life.

There are six skills in Global Perspectives, and you keep growing all of them, year after year:

This unit is about the fifth skill: Collaboration. Most of your Global Perspectives work so far has been something you could do largely on your own: researching, analysing, evaluating and reflecting. Collaboration is different. You cannot collaborate by yourself. It is the skill of getting good things done with other people — agreeing a shared goal, sharing the work fairly, listening closely, handling disagreement well, and finishing something together that no single person could have built alone.

In Stage 8 you go further than before. It is not enough simply to be in a team and be pleasant. This year you will divide roles by thinking carefully about each person's strengths and the time you have; you will make sure the ideas your team puts forward are backed by reasoning and evidence, not just opinion; you will resolve real disagreements and solve problems as they come up; you will give and receive specific feedback; and you will step back and judge honestly how well your team worked, including your own part in it. These are the moves of a genuinely effective team.

Why does this matter beyond school? Almost everything important in the adult world is built by teams. A road is made safer when a community, its drivers and the local authority agree on a plan and act on it. People who collaborate well get chosen for the best work, and they get more done. That is why we practise it here, on purpose, until it becomes natural.
